source_links.title: Location: Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines

text:
Case study: Cagayan de Oro (Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines)
Section: Is there any evidence of a proactive or reactive trigger in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Reactive (primary), with limited pre-existing proactive elements that did not constitute a managed retreat decision.

**Narrative:** The resettlement was overwhelmingly triggered by the actual occurrence of Typhoon Washi in December 2011. All reviewed sources consistently describe the disaster as the trigger: "the disaster became afterward the trigger of resettlement" (Carrasco et al. 2016a, p. 38); "Typhoon Washi has been considered the trigger for a long-time expected resettlement" (Carrasco & Egbelakin 2022, p. 4).

Pre-disaster risk assessments did exist: a 2009 geo-hazard assessment by the Mines and Geosciences Bureau (MGB) identified flood-prone areas along the Cagayan de Oro River, and a 2010 Xavier University study identified specific barangays at risk. However, no pre-disaster relocation action was taken in response to either assessment. Survivors admitted they knew the risks but remained because they had nowhere to go (Carrasco et al. 2016a).

There is a limited proactive element: the LGU had previously purchased land for social housing and emergency use — described in the sources as "land banking" — and had drafted a Relocation Plan before Washi. This pre-existing land availability enabled unusually fast post-disaster housing construction. However, this land acquisition had not translated into any pre-disaster resettlement programme. Notably, a Disaster Risk Reduction Management office in the LGU was only created *after* Washi (Carrasco et al. 2016a), confirming the predominantly reactive institutional posture.

**Coding:** Reactive (primary). The limited proactive element (land banking, draft Relocation Plan) constitutes pre-existing enabling infrastructure rather than a proactive managed retreat decision.

source_links.title: Location: Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines

text:
Case study: Cagayan de Oro (Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines)
Section: Date, Number of Households Affected, Number of Population Affected, Total Funding

**Date:** Primary disaster: 16–17 December 2011. Resettlement programme announced January 2012. First beneficiary transfer: 28 April 2012. Programme ongoing; latest documented activities 2021.

**Number of households affected:** 69,715 families were displaced in Cagayan de Oro (Carrasco et al. 2016a). The resettlement programme targeted a total of 11,225 housing units, of which 9,699 were planned for ADRRS relocation sites. By July 2014: 7,952 units completed; 6,421 occupied (NHA data cited in Carrasco et al. 2016a). After 27 months: 93% of houses completed; 76% occupied (Carrasco & Egbelakin 2022).

**Number of population affected:** 228,576 persons displaced — approximately 40% of Cagayan de Oro's total population (Carrasco et al. 2016a, 2016b; Carrasco & Egbelakin 2022). Total death toll for the region: approximately 1,295 fatalities, 802 missing (Carrasco et al. 2016a). Property damage estimated at approximately PhP 1.3 billion (USD 29.5 million) (Sealza & Sealza 2014).

**Total funding:** No single consolidated programme cost is reported across the reviewed sources. Unit-level costs documented:
- NHA/DSWD-funded units: approximately PhP 110,000 (USD 2,500) per unit. Of this, 64% provided by DSWD (characterised as a donation to beneficiaries); 36% by NHA (status as donation or loan unresolved as of 2014) (Carrasco et al. 2016a).
- FCCC-built prefabricated units: approximately PhP 70,000 (USD 1,550) per unit.
- Oro Habitat (HFHP contractor) units: approximately PhP 90,000 (USD 2,000) per unit.

**Uncertainty:** No consolidated programme-total funding figure is available in the reviewed sources. The primary source identified in the case file (Santiago et al. 2018, DOI: 10.1016/j.ijdrr.2017.11.015) was listed but its full text was not among the provided source documents; additional cost or funding data may exist in that paper.

source_links.title: Location: Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines

text:
Case study: Cagayan de Oro (Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines)
Section: What is the occurrence of the hazard(s) considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Multiple Hazards.

**Narrative:** The primary hazard triggering the resettlement was riverine/flash flooding associated with Tropical Storm Washi. However, multiple hazards are relevant to this case:

1. **Flash flooding / riverine flooding from tropical storm** — primary trigger. The Cagayan de Oro River reached 9.86 m (vs. a normal 2 m) and 41 of 80 barangays were inundated (Carrasco et al. 2016a).
2. **Subsequent typhoon hazard** — Typhoon Bopha (December 2012) affected Cagayan de Oro and led to the discovery of roof-structure deficiencies in a neighbouring settlement (Carrasco et al. 2016a, 2016b).
3. **Landslide/slope instability at resettlement sites** — houses built on hillslopes at Calaanan were severely damaged during rain and typhoon seasons; 37 houses were rendered uninhabitable and residents required secondary relocation (Carrasco et al. 2016a, 2016b).
4. **Earthquake risk** — referenced in the sources as part of the Philippines' multi-hazard context (Carrasco et al. 2016a) and in housing extension safety assessments (Carrasco et al. 2016b). This is background contextual risk, not a driver of the retreat decision.

The Philippines is explicitly described as "a multi-hazard prone country, astride the 'Pacific Ring of Fire' and the 'Typhoon Belt'" (Carrasco et al. 2016a, p. 36).

**Coding:** Multiple Hazards. The primary decision driver was flooding from tropical storm/typhoon. Landslide emerged as a secondary hazard at the resettlement sites themselves. Earthquake is background risk only.

source_links.title: Location: Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines

text:
Case study: Cagayan de Oro (Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines)
Section: What is the origin of the hazards considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Natural Hazard.

**Narrative:** All relevant hazards — tropical storm/typhoon with associated flash flooding, landslides, and seismic risk — are naturally occurring phenomena. The sources note that the Philippines is at high risk from climate change-related events such as increasing typhoon intensity and frequency (Carrasco & Egbelakin 2022), but the specific hazard that triggered the retreat (Typhoon Washi) is framed as a natural disaster event. Climate change is invoked as context for the country's future risk exposure, not as the direct causal driver of the retreat decision. No technological or industrial hazards are identified.

**Coding:** Natural Hazard.

source_links.title: Location: Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines

text:
Case study: Cagayan de Oro (Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines)
Section: Was this hazard considered in the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Riverine/Pluvial Flooding (primary); Hurricane (tropical storm/typhoon); Landslide/Debris Flow (secondary, at resettlement sites); Earthquake (background risk only, not a decision driver).

**Narrative:**

- **Riverine/Pluvial Flooding:** The primary driver of the No-Build Zone declaration and the resettlement programme. The Cagayan de Oro River's catastrophic rise destroyed thousands of riverbank homes.
- **Hurricane (tropical storm/typhoon):** Typhoon Washi and Typhoon Bopha are both documented. The Philippines' typhoon exposure is described as a "permanent threat" (Carrasco et al. 2016a). The codebook notes that the Hurricane category includes "tropical storms and hurricanes (cyclones or typhoons)."
- **Landslide/Debris Flow:** This hazard emerged at the receiving sites rather than the sending sites. Inadequate geo-hazard assessments led to houses being built in landslide-prone areas at Calaanan. Thirty-seven houses were severely damaged and residents relocated.
- **Earthquake:** Referenced in the sources as general Philippines multi-hazard context (Carrasco et al. 2016a) and in the safety assessment of housing extensions (Carrasco et al. 2016b), but is not described as a driver of the resettlement decision.

Coastal flooding, lake flooding, wildfire, volcano, land subsidence, and tsunami are not identified as relevant hazards in the reviewed sources.

**Coding:** Riverine/Pluvial Flooding; Hurricane; Landslide/Debris Flow (secondary, at receiving sites); Earthquake (background context only).

---

source_links.title: Location: Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines

text:
Case study: Cagayan de Oro (Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines)
Section: What was the geographic scale of the MR project?

**Answer:** Neighbourhood (primary operational scale), with city-wide governance and displacement context.

**Narrative:** The displacement affected approximately 40% of Cagayan de Oro's total population, giving the programme a city-wide dimension in terms of scale of impact and governance coordination. However, the retreat itself was implemented at the neighbourhood and site scale: specific riverbank barangays were declared No-Build Zones, and residents were relocated to multiple designated peri-urban resettlement sites (the largest being Calaanan). The programme did not involve the entire city retreating; it targeted informal settlers in specific vulnerable sub-areas. Individual beneficiary selection was household-level; site planning and management was at neighbourhood level.

The codebook does not list a "city-wide" option. The most precise fit for the operational scale is Neighbourhood. The city-wide governance context is noted as a complementary characteristic.

**Coding:** Neighbourhood (primary). The city-wide displacement scale and city-level governance are noted as relevant contextual features, but the operational managed retreat was at neighbourhood/site level. "Entire community" overstates the scope given that only affected sub-populations were relocated.

source_links.title: Location: Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines

text:
Case study: Cagayan de Oro (Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines)
Section: Who or what was retreated?

**Answer:** Individuals and Groups/Neighbourhoods.

**Narrative:** The retreat targeted individual households through a beneficiary selection process (priority given to those with totally destroyed homes, single mothers, large families, people with disabilities). However, the resettlement was also managed at the group/neighbourhood level: residents of specific vulnerable barangays along the riverbanks were collectively targeted, and resettlement sites were organised as new neighbourhood settlements. No infrastructure-only retreat, no industrial asset relocation, and no community-as-a-whole retreat (in the sense of an entire town or city) is described. Approximately 85% of affected households were informal settlers without legal title to their original land.

**Coding:** Individuals; Groups/Neighbourhoods.

source_links.title: Location: Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines

text:
Case study: Cagayan de Oro (Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines)
Section: What is the focus or scope of the MR project?

**Answer:** Community buyout/retreat (primary); Individual buyout/retreat (secondary, for household-level allocation process).

**Narrative:** The dominant approach was state-led collective resettlement of informal settlers from No-Build Zones to government-constructed housing in designated relocation sites. The programme operated at the community/neighbourhood scale in terms of planning, site development, and housing construction, making "Community buyout/retreat" the closest codebook category — while acknowledging that this was a state-led forced resettlement rather than a voluntary market buyout. Since approximately 85% of affected households were informal settlers without legal title to their original land, no monetary compensation for property was provided. Instead, beneficiaries received allocated housing units through usufruct arrangements.

Beneficiary selection operated at the individual household level, making "Individual buyout/retreat" a relevant secondary category for this component of the process. There is no evidence of leasebacks, easements, buffers, or managed realignment of infrastructure in the reviewed sources.

**Coding:** Community buyout/retreat (primary); Individual buyout/retreat (secondary, for beneficiary selection). **Note:** This was a state-led forced resettlement of informal settlers, not a market-based voluntary buyout. The community buyout/retreat code is applied in the sense of collective relocation rather than a traditional North American property buyout model.

source_links.title: Location: Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines

text:
Case study: Cagayan de Oro (Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines)
Section: What legal constraints or requirements were identified during the MR decision process?

**Answer:** Legal authority over retreat; Relevant regulations/acts; Land acquisition; Title(s) transfer; Land rezoning; Retreat land development; Compliance & enforcement.

**Narrative:**

- **Legal authority over retreat:** The LGU, acting through the LIAC chaired by the city mayor, assumed primary authority for declaring No-Build Zones and managing resettlement. The NHA and DSWD provided the national legal and operational framework. The LIAC functioned as the mediator between local and national government offices and humanitarian and private sectors (Carrasco et al. 2016a).

- **Relevant regulations/acts:** Multiple frameworks were invoked:
  - *Philippine Water Code*: establishes a 3-metre easement along rivers, underpinning the No-Build Zone declaration (Carrasco et al. 2016a).
  - *National Building Code of the Philippines* (DPWH): regulated minimum construction standards.
  - *Minimum Design Standards and Requirements for Economic and Socialized Housing Projects* (HLURB BP 220): set housing design parameters including minimum floor area.
  - *Civil Code of the Philippines* (Republic Act 386, Articles 562–612): defined the usufruct arrangement (Carrasco et al. 2016b).
  - *Philippine Electrical Code; National Plumbing Code; Sanitation Code of the Philippines*: service provision standards.
  - *National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management framework*.
  - *Ordinance No. 14125-2021* (City of Cagayan de Oro): declared river boundary areas as Regulated Land-Use Zones as part of the FRIMP-CDOR (Carrasco & Egbelakin 2022).

- **Land acquisition:** Pre-disaster LGU land banking (purchase of land for social housing and emergency use) was critical to rapid post-disaster housing construction. Post-disaster, the LGU continued acquiring land to fulfil outstanding housing needs (Carrasco et al. 2016a). Some private institutions donated land.

- **Title(s) transfer:** A critical legal constraint throughout the programme. Residents were granted usufruct rights (usually 25–50 years of occupancy) rather than formal ownership. As of 2014, "there is no legal framework to transfer these properties to beneficiaries" (Carrasco et al. 2016a, p. 44). Residents "do not have formal ownership of the houses neither of the lot" (Carrasco et al. 2016b, p. 103). By 2019, government officials had begun discussing possible ownership transfer; by late 2021, some residents had been granted titling, but this process is constrained by a national quota that prevents all residents from receiving titling at once (Carrasco & Egbelakin 2022). The lack of secure tenure was identified across sources as a major ongoing vulnerability.

- **Land rezoning:** No-Build Zones were declared along the riverbanks, effectively prohibiting residential use in flood-prone areas. A 2021 city ordinance formally declared river boundary areas as Regulated Land-Use Zones (Carrasco & Egbelakin 2022). The criteria for No-Build Zone delineation were also noted as inconsistent with the city's zoning plans and lacking clear risk-level definitions (Carrasco et al. 2016b).

- **Retreat land development:** Usufruct agreements prohibited beneficiaries from returning to original riverbank settlements. The vacated land was not described as having been actively redeveloped or ecologically restored in the reviewed sources.

- **Compliance & enforcement:** The prohibition on housing extensions was largely unenforced; local government staff chose not to enforce restrictions to avoid conflict with communities, and residents reportedly built extensions during weekends (Carrasco & Egbelakin 2022). Residents who voluntarily abandoned houses or returned to original sites had usufruct agreements terminated (Carrasco & Egbelakin 2022). Building permit supervision during construction was described as focused on counting completed units rather than construction quality (Carrasco et al. 2016a).

- **Litigation:** No evidence of formal litigation in the reviewed sources.

**Coding:** Legal authority over retreat; Relevant regulations/acts; Land acquisition; Title(s) transfer; Land rezoning; Retreat land development; Compliance & enforcement.

source_links.title: Location: Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines

text:
Case study: Cagayan de Oro (Cagayan de Oro, Northern Mindanao, Philippines)
Section: What were the funding sources for the MR project?

**Answer:** Multiple funders: Federal (national government agencies), Local/Municipal, NGOs, International aid, Private sector.

**Narrative:**
- **Federal (national government):** NHA and DSWD were the primary national government funders of housing construction. DSWD provided 64% of per-unit costs (approximately PhP 70,400 / USD 1,600 per unit) characterised as a donation to beneficiaries; NHA provided 36% (approximately PhP 39,600 / USD 900 per unit), with the status of this funding — whether grant or loan — unresolved as of 2014 (Carrasco et al. 2016a).
- **Local/Municipal:** The LGU of Cagayan de Oro owned and managed the majority of resettlement land and was responsible for site development (roads, drainage, water supply) (Carrasco et al. 2016a).
- **NGOs:** Habitat for Humanity Philippines (with support from Habitat for Humanity International), Gawad Kalinga, and Oro Habitat funded and built housing units. Catholic Relief Services (CRS) and IOM funded transitional shelter programmes (Carrasco et al. 2016a).
- **International aid:** IOM, CRS, UN-Habitat, and UNHCR are documented as involved in coordination of early shelter assistance and transitional shelter (Carrasco et al. 2016a). UNICEF, the World Food Programme, and German Doctors provided immediate relief goods and services in the initial humanitarian response (Sealza & Sealza 2014).
- **Private sector:** The Filipino-Chinese Chamber of Commerce (FCCC) — a private-sector entity — provided funding and directly organised construction of 300 prefabricated housing units at Calaanan. Some private institutions donated land for emergency shelters or permanent housing (Carrasco et al. 2016a, 2016b). GK Shell was partially funded by the corporation Shell (Carrasco & Egbelakin 2022).

**Coding:** Multiple funders; Federal (NHA, DSWD); Local/Municipal (LGU); NGOs (HFHP, GK, OH, CRS, IOM); International aid (IOM, CRS, UN-Habitat, UNHCR; UNICEF/WFP/German Doctors for initial relief); Private sector (FCCC, Shell).
